session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their everyday lives — where they go, what they eat, who they eat with — rather than as subjects of a study about gender or food ideology. The collective identity is ordinary men with real food habits and social lives, not advocates or critics of any particular diet. This keeps the register grounded in lived experience rather than opinion-performance.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): highest risk of socially desirable or performatively 'enlightened' answers — men may either overstate gender's influence to seem self-aware, or dismiss it defensively. Behavioural grounding and specific-moment probes will be essential.

Social acceptability of plant-based eating and gendered food meanings (Sections 3–5): participants may converge quickly on comfortable shared positions ('it's just personal choice'); need to surface tensions between stated attitudes and actual behaviour in social settings.

What would need to change for plant-based eating (Section 4): risk of abstract or idealised answers; need to anchor responses in specific real-life constraints — logistics, social pressure, taste — rather than hypothetical willingness.

Making plant-based foods more appealing (Section 5): risk of marketing-speak or generic answers; probe toward personal specificity and moments where existing plant-based food has succeeded or failed for them personally.

known_risk_conditions: High social desirability risk throughout: men discussing gender and food may perform progressive self-awareness rather than report real behaviour. Use behavioural grounding ('think of a specific time...') especially in Sections 3 and 4.
Early consensus risk on gender question: group may quickly land on 'no, gender doesn't really affect it' and move on. Plan an invite_dissent or sharpening condition ready if this happens.
Plant-based sections may drift toward abstract product feedback rather than personal and social meaning — keep probes anchored to real experience and social context, not consumer preference research.
Group may avoid discomfort around masculinity norms by staying in ironic or jokey register — monitor emotional_signals for deflection via humour and probe gently beneath it when it appears.

No researcher notes flagging personal sensitivities — treat as a standard-risk group, but remain attentive to signals of dietary restriction (religious, medical) that could make certain questions feel exclusionary.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro and opening): very light touch — warm, open, minimal intervention. Let rapport build naturally. Only probe in the intro if something emotionally or analytically striking surfaces. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): moderate directivity — ground in specific behaviours, begin surfacing social context for later. Sections 3–5 (main topic): highest directivity — push for specificity, surface contradictions, challenge easy consensus, use behavioural grounding and hypotheticals. Be prepared to slow down the group if they race through these sections without depth. Section 6 (closing): return to light touch — genuine invitation for anything missed, no reopening of fully-covered ground.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) are the research core and receive the heaviest allocation (~55% combined). Context sections (1, 2) are moderately weighted — they warm up participants and surface material that feeds into main topics. Intro (0) and closing (6) receive minimal allocations. Turn budgets are estimated at roughly 80–100 words per participant turn average.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the social infrastructure of male friendship — specifically how groups organise time together and what sustains or disrupts those patterns. An early routine-versus-flexibility tension (pub standing arrangement vs. ad-hoc plans) was reframed mid-section by life-stage logistics: parenthood, geography, and partner schedules emerged as the real structural forces. The section closed on adaptation as the key variable — whether friendships survive constraint depends on willingness to change the format rather than preserve the original one.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening moves were hands-off, letting Sam and Bilal develop a productive disagreement without interruption. The intervention at turn 7 was designed to widen the sample before the binary hardened, and it worked — Noah triangulated, Henry introduced life-stage complexity, and the conversation deepened without moderator steering. The closing prompt to Connor before transitioning was functional but slightly rushed; Connor never actually responded, leaving one voice unheard at section end.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section added a single clarifying extension to the previous section's life-stage and logistics theme: urban geography as a structural barrier compounding other constraints. The commute-as-tax framing introduced the idea that distance is baked into city life before any other factor arrives, making intentionality not just a personality trait but a near-necessity. No new thematic territory opened; the section functioned as a closing elaboration before the topic shift.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator allowed Connor — the voice left unheard at the previous section's close — to complete the thread before pivoting, which was the right repair. The transition to food decision-making was abrupt and unexplained; no bridge was offered between friendship logistics and eating habits, risking a jarring gear-change for participants. Validating Connor's point briefly before moving was adequate but the pivot itself could have been warmer or better framed.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on gendered food performance — the unspoken pressure to order certain things in male company. A productive internal/external pressure distinction emerged: is the constraint genuinely social or self-imposed habit? This bifurcated further around familiarity: established groups permit more freedom than newer ones. The section's sharpest move was Connor's salad/vegan distinction — salad is neutral food choice, plant-based eating is a legible identity statement, and that statement carries more social weight on men than women.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening gender-and-food prompt landed well — Bilal took it seriously and set a candid tone. Letting the Henry-Bilal debate run without intervention was the right call; it produced the internal/external distinction organically. Direct addresses to Noah and Connor were timely and both yielded genuine contributions. The pivot from Connor's 'not wanting to be a hassle' framing to the plant-based question was the section's best move — it sharpened the enquiry considerably. The closing transition to practical barriers was clean and well-bridged.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the barriers discussion by distinguishing logistics from relational friction — with the central insight being that family dynamics don't just complicate food choices, they make practical change unsustainable over time. A Bilal-Noah-Sam thread interrogated whether that tension ever genuinely resolves or merely goes quiet. Henry introduced a structural variable: whether you're shifting alone or alongside others. Connor closed with something distinct — not a barrier but an absence of motivation, framing inertia itself as a friction mode.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The approach was mostly reactive amplification — surfacing Bilal's relational-wear-down framing, then directing Henry and Connor to extend it rather than letting the Bilal-Sam debate exhaust itself. Both direct addresses landed well: Henry triangulated the tension productively, Connor reframed the section's question entirely. The closing pivot to 'what would make the case for it' used Connor's inertia observation as a legitimate bridge rather than forcing a topic shift — cleaner than some earlier transitions.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reframed the earlier 'no self-interested hook' insight through a sharper distinction: between genuinely not seeing a reason and seeing it but choosing not to act. A Henry-Noah exchange forced that clarification productively — Noah and Connor ultimately admitted they perceive the hook but accept the contradiction rather than take it. Bilal then introduced a critical counterpoint: his friction is relational and ongoing, not a low-stakes contradiction he can simply sit with.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were surfacing the Noah-Connor convergence and then using it as a deliberate contrast to pull Bilal back in. Both worked — the first sharpened a fuzzy insight into something more honest, the second produced Bilal's clearest articulation of the session. The closing open invitation before time was adequate but slightly abrupt; more space there might have surfaced something from Sam, who had been quiet throughout this section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section surfaced a sharp epistemological challenge: whether naming a structural problem constitutes meaningful progress when nothing about the situation changes. Henry's self-correction, and Bilal's refusal to accept understanding as proxy for resolution, produced the session's most honest moment — an explicit acknowledgement that some constraints have no solution and that treating analytical clarity as improvement is itself a kind of evasion.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator stayed almost entirely absent, correctly reading that the Henry-Bilal exchange was self-completing and needed no steering. The closing statement matched the section's emotional register — resisting false resolution, naming the conversation's candour without overstating it. The risk is that Sam, Noah, and Connor were effectively absent from this final section, but disrupting the Henry-Bilal thread to rebalance participation would have cost more than it gained.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. I'm the moderator for this session — my job is basically to listen and ask questions, so this is very much your conversation, not mine. We've got about 45 minutes together and we're going to be recorded for research purposes, so just a heads-up on that. In terms of how this works: I'm genuinely interested in what you actually think and do — not what sounds right or what you think I'm looking for, because honestly there are no right answers here. If something someone else says connects with your experience, jump in — you don't need to wait for me to ask you directly. And if something doesn't match your experience at all, that's just as useful to hear. The only thing I'd ask is to be respectful of each other and try to keep things reasonably concise so everyone gets a chance to talk. Okay — let's just get started. Let's go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
Yeah, hi everyone. I'm Connor, I'm from London — Greater London, so not central but around the area. I'm 34. That's about it really, nothing too exciting. Pleased to be here though.

Great, good to meet you all — Sam, Noah, Henry, Bilal, Connor. Let's get into it. Think about the places you actually go with your male friends — a pub, a park, someone's place, wherever it is for you. What's your go-to spot, and what keeps you coming back to it?

Yeah, so for me it's definitely the local pub. There's one just down the road from where I am in the suburbs here, and that's where we meet up pretty much every other week, sometimes more often depending on what's going on. 

I think what keeps us coming back is just... it's convenient, innit. It's close by, so no one's got to travel far. And the staff know us at this point, so there's a bit of familiarity there. You can just turn up without having to plan anything too elaborate. Plus it's decent for a chat without being too noisy, which sounds daft but it matters when you're trying to actually talk to people rather than just shouting over music. And there's always something on the telly if the conversation dies, so it doesn't feel awkward.

Yeah, but that's not really... I mean, fair enough if that works for you, but for me and my mates it's completely different. We're not really pub people, to be honest. Like, we'll go sometimes, but it's not the go-to thing.

Most of the time we're either round someone's gaff or we're doing something specific, you know? Like if there's a match on, we'll go to the ground or watch it together somewhere. Or we'll just be at someone's place with a few beers, playing FIFA or whatever, just messing about. That's where we actually hang out.

I think maybe it depends on your age a bit as well. I'm 32, so I'm not young young, but I think for a lot of lads around my age in the city, the pub thing — that whole casual drop-in situation — it's just not how we work anymore. Life's busier, innit. You've got to coordinate stuff. So it tends to be more planned, round someone's, or it's got to be part of something else, like the football.

No, I get what you're saying about coordination, but I'd actually say it's the opposite for us. Like, the pub works because it doesn't need much planning. We don't have to sit there texting back and forth for three weeks trying to find a time when everyone's free at someone's house. We just sort of know — Thursday night, we're down the pub. Job done.

Though I mean, maybe that's because we're not trying to do anything specific, you know? We're not waiting for a match or whatever. We're just there to have a few pints and chat. That's the whole point of it, really. Whereas if you're organizing people round someone's place, everyone's got to make sure they're free and all that.

I don't know if it's age though, honestly. I reckon it's more just what your mates are into and where you live. Like, I'm in the suburbs — the pub's on my doorstep basically. If I was in the city center maybe it'd be different, but out here it just makes sense.

Fair point, actually. You're right about that — if you've got a standing thing going, Thursday night at the pub, then yeah, no one has to faff about organizing it. That does take the hassle out of it.

But I think what you're saying kind of proves my point a bit differently, you know? Like, your thing works because you've all just agreed that's what you do. It's routine. Whereas with my lot, we're not really into that. Some lads want to go to the match, some want to just chill at someone's, some want to go out somewhere. It's more... fragmented, I suppose.

So it's not really about the suburbs versus the city, like you said. It's more that your group's agreed on one thing and you stick with it, which is fair enough. But not everyone operates like that. Some friend groups just don't have that one locked-in activity, you know what I mean? We're more... we'll sort it out when we see each other or when something's on.

Yeah, but I wouldn't call ours rigid though. Like, we're not sitting there saying "this is the only place we ever go." We do other stuff too — we've been to watch games, we've had people round, we've gone out for a night out in town. But having that one thing, that standing arrangement, it doesn't limit anything. If someone wants to do something different, we do it. It's just nice to have something that's there without having to think about it.

I think your lot sounds more like... you're making plans each time? Which is fine, but that's not fragmented, that's just how you prefer it. I just think calling the routine thing rigid makes it sound like we're stuck doing the same thing every week when we're not, really. We just happen to like the pub and we know we can always find each other there.

Sam and Bilal, you've basically laid out two different things there — one where there's a standing arrangement that just happens, and one where it's more sort of sorted out as you go. Noah, Henry, Connor — does either of those sound like your setup, or is it something else entirely?

Yeah, I think I'm somewhere in the middle, to be honest. Like, I've got the Thursday thing with some lads — we just go down to the local, it's dead easy, no one has to think about it. But then I've got other mates, right, and it's nothing like that. We might go to someone's place, or we'll catch a match if there's something on, or we just sort of... text and see what happens.

So I don't think it's either/or, is it? Sam, your routine thing — that's not rigid just because it's routine. And Bilal, you're not fragmented just because you're flexible. It's just... different groups work different ways. I've got both going on at the same time and it works fine. 

The Thursday lads, we've got that standing thing, but if someone says "nah, let's do something different this week," we just do it. It's not like the pub owns us. But it's nice knowing it's there if you can't be bothered planning anything. And with my other mates, yeah, we sort it out as we go, but that doesn't mean it's chaotic or anything. It just means we need a bit more coordination sometimes.

Think it comes down to who you're with, doesn't it? Different groups of mates, different arrangements. Nothing wrong with either way.

Yeah, Noah's hit on something real there about having multiple groups with different setups. But I reckon there's something about the life stage and actual logistics in Birmingham that hasn't quite been said.

Like, I'm with Sam on the routine thing — I've got mates I see regular down the local, and it's just... you know where you are. But what I've noticed, right, is that shifts depending on what's happening in people's lives. My situation's probably closer to what Sam's describing with the routine, but I've seen how it shifts when you've got kids or when your mates start coupling up. 

I've got a few lads who used to be at the pub every week with us, and then one of them had a kid, moved out a bit further, and suddenly he can't just drop in Thursday nights anymore. His missus is working, he's got to sort childcare, whatever. So now when he does meet up with us, it's got to be planned properly, or it's round someone's place where the kid can come along and mess about.

And I think that's the bit that's maybe getting a bit lost in this — it's not just about whether you like routine or you like flexibility. It's about what your actual week looks like, you know? Living in the city center versus the suburbs makes a difference, but so does whether you're single, partnered up, got kids, got a job that knocks you out by Friday. That changes what's actually doable.

Yeah, Henry, that's... that's actually spot on. That's what I'm starting to see with my Thursday lads right now. A couple of them have got kids now, and it's changing how the whole thing works.

Like, it used to be dead simple — everyone just showed up. But now one of them, his partner's doing shifts, so some weeks he can't even make it because he's got to be home with the kids. And when he does come, he's not staying late or anything, you know? He's got to get back. So it's not really about whether he prefers routine or flexibility anymore — it's just... he can't do what he used to do.

And I reckon that's going to shift more, to be honest. Another mate's about to become a dad any month now, so I'm expecting the same thing. We're all kind of aware it's coming. It doesn't mean we're not going to see each other, but it might not be Thursday nights at the pub as much. It'll probably be more what Henry's saying — planned things, or maybe round someone's place where the kids can just... be there.

So I think you're right that it's not really about preference in the way Sam and Bilal were talking about it. It's bigger than that. It's just life, innit. You can prefer routines all you want, but if you've got a one-year-old at home, that preference doesn't matter much. You've got to work with what you've actually got going on.

Right, but that's the thing — it doesn't have to mean Thursday nights die, does it? It just... transforms. I've got mates who've managed to keep something going even with kids. It's different, yeah, but it's still there.

Like, one of my lads, he couldn't do the regular pub thing anymore once his kids came along. But instead of just losing touch or waiting for some mythical day when he's got childcare sorted, we shifted it. Sometimes he brings the kids round someone's place on a Sunday afternoon, we've got a few beers, they're running about playing with toys or whatever. It's not the same as Thursday night down the local, but it's still... you're still in it, you know? You're still seeing each other regularly.

And I think that matters more than people realize. Because what I've seen happen is, if you just let it drop because someone's had a kid or moved further out, you lose the thread a bit. Then when they finally get a free evening or whatever, it feels awkward to get back into it. You've drifted.

But if you actually adjust how you do it — like, okay, it's Sunday afternoon with kids in tow instead of Thursday night just the lads — you don't break that connection. You stay in each other's lives through it. That's the bit that takes a bit of effort, though. You've got to be willing to shift how you do it rather than just assuming the whole thing's finished.

Yeah, that point about adapting rather than just letting it drop — that's come through from a few of you. Connor, did you want to add anything quickly before we move on? And then I want to shift us onto something else.

Yeah, I mean Henry's point about adapting — that really does resonate with me. I've seen exactly that happen, you know? The Sunday afternoon thing with kids is real.

But I think there's also the commute factor, especially out here in Greater London. It's not just about having kids, it's that even if you do manage to organize something, getting across London to meet up is just... it takes time, doesn't it? Like, if I want to see a mate who's on the other side of the city, it's not just popping down to the local. It's an hour on the tube or whatever, depending on where they've ended up.

So I reckon that's part of why the routine thing works better for some people — you're all local to something. But out here, you're spread out already. Add kids into that and it gets even harder to maintain things the way you used to. You've got to be more intentional about it, like Henry said. But yeah, the distance thing is a real barrier that's just... baked in, I suppose.

Yeah, the geography of it is real — when you're already spread across a big city, the distance becomes its own kind of tax on top of everything else. Good. Let's shift to something related but a bit different. We've been talking about where you go and who you see — let's talk about what you actually eat. How do you decide what to eat? Just on an ordinary day, what goes into that decision?

Yeah, I think Henry's right about that — the routine thing doesn't lock you in, it actually gives you something to hold onto when life changes. Because like, if you've got that standing arrangement, even when circumstances shift, you've got a reason to keep showing up and adapt it rather than just... letting it fade.

We haven't had the kids situation yet with our lot, but I can see how it'd work. Having that Thursday thing means you're not starting from scratch trying to coordinate something new every time. You're just going "right, this Thursday's going to look different, but we're still doing it." Takes the thinking out of it, doesn't it?

Connor's point about distance is fair though. I suppose being out in the suburbs, we're all sort of clustered around the same area anyway, so that helps. If we were all scattered around different parts of the region, it'd be a nightmare.

Nice one. Let's shift gears a bit — I want to ask you all something that might need a bit more thought. Thinking about what you actually eat day to day, do you reckon your gender shapes that at all? Not what you think it should do — more whether, in practice, being a man has ever made a difference to what you order, what you'd admit to eating, or what you'd feel comfortable with in front of other people.

Yeah, I think there's definitely something there, to be honest. Like, I wouldn't say it's massive, but it's... it's real.

I mean, with my mates, there's definitely stuff you wouldn't order or you wouldn't really talk about. Like, if I'm honest, I quite like a salad, right? But I'm not going to sit there and order one in front of the lads and make a big thing about it. Not because anyone's going to give me proper grief about it, but it's just... you know what I mean? There's an unspoken thing.

Or like, I'll eat something at home that I wouldn't necessarily order out with mates. Pasta, nice home-cooked stuff — that's fine on your own or with your missus or family. But when you're out with the boys, there's a bit of... you want to order something that just doesn't look like you're making an effort, or being fussy, or whatever. Like a burger or a steak or something. Simple, doesn't need explaining.

I don't know if that's masculinity or just what your mates are into, but yeah, there's definitely a thing where you're aware of what you're ordering and how it'll come across. It's not like anyone's said anything to me, but you just pick up on it, you know?

Yeah, I know what you mean, Bilal. But I think there's a distinction there between actual mate pressure and just... internalised stuff, you know?

Like, yeah, I've clocked that same thing — you're not ordering a salad with the lads because it feels a bit precious or like you're making a statement about it. But here's the thing: I've actually done it. Ordered a salad, or gone for something lighter, and literally nothing happened. No one said anything, no one took the piss. And I realized I was basically creating that pressure myself.

Which ties back to what we were saying earlier about being intentional. With my mates, the ones I see regularly — Thursday night lads or whatever — we've kind of got to a point where it's just... you order what you want. And I think that's because we've been around long enough that you don't have to prove anything anymore. You're not still performing what you think a bloke should be like.

But I reckon if you're always worried about how it looks, you don't get there. You stay stuck in that unspoken thing. Whereas if you just order the salad once and realize nobody cares, it shifts, doesn't it? The pressure doesn't actually come from them — it comes from you thinking they're thinking it.

That said, maybe that's easier for me because I'm not in a massive group where there's new faces all the time. If you're always meeting different people, yeah, maybe that pressure's a bit more real because you don't know them well enough to just relax into it.

Right, but that's kind of the point though, innit? You've got that established thing — Thursday night with the same lads. You've been going long enough that you don't have to perform anymore. Fair enough, that works for you.

But I'm not always in that situation. Like, I might be meeting up with a mix of people, or someone's brought a mate I don't know that well, or it's just... you're not always in that comfortable space where you've been going for years and everyone knows each other. Sometimes you're still proving yourself a bit, whether that's conscious or not.

And yeah, maybe some of it is self-imposed, but it's not like I'm making it up out of thin air, you know? It's a real thing that exists around you when you're in certain situations. I might order what I want with my closest mates, but if I'm in a bigger group or newer people are there, it's different. You're still kind of... aware of how you come across.

So I don't think it's just about being brave enough to order a salad once. It's about the actual context you're in. And that context changes depending on who you're with and how long you've known them.

Yeah, okay, that's fair. You're right — context matters, and I was maybe oversimplifying it a bit.

But I think I've been conflating two different things without really sitting with where the actual tension is. Like, there's the pressure from new people or bigger groups — that's real, that's external pressure. But then there's also the stuff I do to myself even with my regular lads, and those aren't quite the same thing, are they?

Like, I said I've ordered a salad with no problem, but if I'm honest, there's still times when I don't. And I'm not always sure if that's because I actually think someone'll judge me or because I'm just... used to not doing it. It's become automatic. That's different from walking into a room full of people you don't know and thinking "I better order a burger so I don't look soft."

The thing is, if you don't actually test that assumption with your regular mates — if you just keep performing the same way because you've always done it — you don't really know if it's them or you, do you? And that matters because it affects what you can actually change.

With Bilal's point about new groups or bigger setups, yeah, that's harder. You're genuinely more exposed. But with your actual mates, your core people — I reckon there's something worth trying to shift there. Otherwise you're just... forever managing an image that maybe doesn't even need managing anymore.
Noah, I'm curious where you land on all of this — does any of what Henry and Bilal are describing feel familiar from your end?

Yeah, I mean... it's a bit of both, innit? Like, with my Thursday lads, I've known most of them for ages, so it's pretty relaxed. I'll order what I want, no one's bothered. But Henry's right that I probably still do sometimes just go for something dead normal because it's easier, you know? Not because I think they'll care, just because... it's what you do.

But then Bilal's point about context — that's real too. Like, if we're out and someone's brought someone new, or we're in a bigger group, yeah, there's a bit of that awareness. You're not going to order something mad and then spend ten minutes explaining what it is or why you're having it.

I suppose the thing I'm thinking about is what Henry said about testing that stuff with your actual mates. Because I've not really... I don't think I've tested it much, have I? I just kind of know what I normally order and I stick with it. Whether that's because I genuinely prefer it or because I'm just used to not ordering other things, I couldn't really tell you.

With the kids thing we were talking about earlier, though — it's making me wonder if I'll have more of that awareness creep in, you know? Because once you've got a kid, you're around different people more. Parents, that sort of thing. And maybe you care a bit more about how you come across because it's not just your mates anymore.
Connor, you've been quiet on this one — where do you land?

Yeah, I mean... I think there's something to what they're all saying, but honestly I'm not sure I think about it that much day to day. Like, I'll order what I want usually. If I'm hungry for a salad, I'll get a salad. Don't really feel self-conscious about it.

But I suppose if I'm being real, there's maybe a bit of that awareness there that I don't necessarily clock until someone brings it up like this. Like, if we're out with a new group or whatever, you probably do just default to something safe, something that doesn't need a story around it. Not because anyone's said anything, just... it's easier, innit?

I think for me it's less about the salad thing and more just about not being a hassle. You don't want to be the person who's difficult about what they're eating or picky or whatever. So you just order something straightforward and get on with it. Whether that's got anything to do with being a bloke, I'm not sure. Could just be me not wanting to be annoying.

That's interesting, Connor — the 'not wanting to be a hassle' thing. Let me throw something at the whole group off the back of that. When you think about specific types of food — vegetarian stuff, vegan, plant-based — do those feel gendered to you in any way? Like, would ordering something like that carry a different weight than just ordering a salad?

Yeah, actually — now you say it like that, there's... yeah, there's definitely a difference, innit. Like, a salad is just food. But if you said you were vegan or you were ordering vegan stuff specifically, that feels different. That feels like you're making a statement about something, you know?

I think I was glossing over that a minute ago when I said it was just about not being a hassle. Because it's not quite the same, is it? Like, ordering a salad because you fancy it — no one cares. But saying "oh, I'm vegan" or "I don't eat meat" — that's got more baggage attached to it somehow. It feels like you're either doing it for environmental reasons or ethics or whatever, and then suddenly it's a whole thing. You're making it about something bigger than just what you feel like eating.

And yeah, I reckon that does feel more gendered than just picking salad. Because it's like... a bloke doing that stands out a bit more, doesn't it? You notice it. Whereas a woman ordering vegan, it's just... expected almost. Less weird about it.

I haven't really done it myself, if I'm honest. There's probably a bit of that in there — not wanting to be the one guy who's... I don't know, made a conscious choice about it in a way that shows. Even if rationally I know most people wouldn't care.

Connor, that's a pretty sharp distinction — salad is just food, but vegan or plant-based feels like a statement, and that statement lands differently depending on whether it's a bloke or a woman making it. Does that ring true for the rest of you? Is there something specifically different about the plant-based or vegan thing compared to just what you order?

Yeah, Connor's hit on something there. There's a difference, innit. A salad is just... a salad. But saying you're vegan or whatever, that does feel like you're declaring something about yourself. It's not just about the food anymore.

And I think that's even more loaded when you start thinking about becoming a parent, to be honest. Because then it's not just your choice anymore, is it? Like, if I went vegan tomorrow, that's me, fair enough. But one of my mates who's about to have a kid — if he decided that was something he wanted to do, suddenly he's not just making a choice for himself. He's potentially making it for his kid too, which is a whole different thing. And that's going to get... I don't know, more questions asked about it probably.

With my Thursday lads, if one of them just started ordering vegan stuff, I don't think anyone would give him proper grief. But there'd be more of a... awareness of it, you know? More of a "oh, right, is that a thing now?" Whereas if someone just orders a salad one week, it's nothing.

And Connor's right that it probably does land differently on a bloke. Because it feels more deliberate somehow. Like you've made an active decision about something, rather than just happening to fancy what you're having. And maybe that's tied up with the whole masculinity thing we were talking about earlier — like, there's still this thing where men aren't supposed to be too intentional about their choices in a visible way. You're just supposed to want a burger, not think about why you're eating what you're eating.

Noah, that last bit — men aren't supposed to be too visibly intentional about what they eat — that's a good place to hang onto. Let's take that into the next bit, because it connects directly to what I want to ask you all now. Imagine you actually decided to go properly plant-based — not just ordering a salad here and there, but making a real shift. What would need to change in your life for that to actually work? Not just theoretically — what's the real friction?

Right, so here's the thing — this isn't just about whether your mates will judge you. That's one bit of it, yeah, but there's actual practical stuff that gets in the way.

Like, work lunches. I grab something at lunch most days, and options around here are... they're not great if you're actually trying to do plant-based properly. It's not like I'm being picky — there's just not much there. It's either a salad or nothing, and sometimes not even that. So you'd have to start bringing stuff from home, which means planning, which means extra effort. And that's every single day, not just when you're out with mates.

Then there's the family thing. My mum still does Sunday dinner sometimes, and if I went vegan, that becomes a whole conversation, doesn't it? She'd take it as a criticism of what she cooks. And my older relatives would definitely have opinions. You'd spend the whole time defending yourself instead of just... eating.

And honestly, there's the cost thing too. Plant-based options out, or proper versions of stuff — it's more expensive usually. So if you're going out with lads and everyone's getting something cheap, you're either paying more or you're still just grabbing a salad.

So it's not really about one mate giving you grief. It's that it changes how you function day to day in ways that are actually annoying. That's the real barrier, I reckon. Not the masculinity stuff — just the logistics of actually doing it.

Bilal's drawing a distinction there between the social judgement side of it and the actual day-to-day logistics — access, planning, cost, the family stuff. Does that map onto what others of you were thinking, or are your friction points somewhere different?

Yeah, but I think what Bilal's brushing past a bit — and maybe this is just me — is that the family stuff isn't really the same as the logistics, is it? Like, yeah, it's practical that your mum makes Sunday dinner, but it's not actually about the logistics of it. It's about how she's going to read it.

Because if I went vegan and it was just about meal planning and bringing stuff to work, that'd be fine. My Thursday lads wouldn't care, I could sort my lunches. But it's the family thing that's different. It's not just Sunday dinner with my mum — it's that if I made that choice, suddenly I'm saying something about how she does things, or what she cares about. And that matters in a way that your mates don't, you know?

And actually, now that I'm thinking about the kids thing — because a couple of my lads are going to be parents — it's even more complicated. Because once you've got a kid, your choices aren't just about you anymore. If you decided to go vegan, you're also deciding that for your kid, at least initially.
